fields.foundation: The Qing Empire originated among the Jurchen people of Manchuria, a confederation of clans living in the forested river valleys north-east of the Great Wall. Between 1583 and 1616 the chieftain Nurhaci united them, turning a fragmented tribal society into a military and political power able to challenge the faltering Ming dynasty, which had governed China for nearly three centuries. Nurhaci’s instrument was the Banner system, begun with four banners in 1601 and expanded to eight by 1615. It divided the Jurchen population into colour-coded units that served at once as fighting formations, census registers and social structures, and it became the framework of the Qing state. In 1616 he proclaimed the Later Jin dynasty, and in 1618 he declared war on the Ming. His son Hong Taiji renamed the people “Manchu” in 1635, distancing them from the Jurchen Jin dynasty that had once ruled northern China, and proclaimed the Qing dynasty in 1636, presenting it as a legitimate successor within the Chinese imperial tradition. The opening came in 1644, when the Ming general Wu Sangui, facing the rebel army of Li Zicheng, which had just seized Beijing, allowed Manchu forces through the Shanhai Pass. Under the regent Dorgon, the Qing moved quickly: they captured Beijing, enthroned the young Shunzhi Emperor as ruler of China and began decades of campaigns against Ming loyalist resistance in the south. Two later victories completed the conquest. The Kangxi Emperor suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (1673–1681), led by powerful Chinese generals who had been granted semi-autonomous southern domains for supporting the conquest, and the Qing conquest of Taiwan from the Ming loyalist regime of the Zheng family followed in 1683. The Qing were then the unchallenged rulers of the most populous empire on earth.
fields.socioeconomy: The Qing Empire governed the most populous agrarian economy in the world, and one of the most productive. Its finances rested on the taxation of agriculture, which fed a population that grew from perhaps 150 million around 1700 to over 400 million by the mid-nineteenth century. This growth was aided by long internal peace and by New World crops, particularly maize, sweet potatoes and peanuts, which extended cultivation into previously marginal hill and upland territories. The Kangxi Emperor froze the poll-tax quota in 1712, and the Yongzheng Emperor’s reforms of the 1720s merged the poll tax into the land tax and regularised the surcharges that had funded local government. These measures simplified fiscal administration, curbed corruption and produced stable revenues that later funded the Qianlong Emperor’s military campaigns. Extensive commercial networks linked China’s regional economies. The Yangtze River system and the Grand Canal were the main routes, carrying grain, silk, cotton, porcelain and tea between producing regions and consuming centres. The Canton System, formalised in 1757, restricted Western maritime trade to the single port of Guangzhou, where it was managed through licensed Chinese merchant houses, the Cohong. This policy of commercial containment brought in substantial customs revenue and kept the terms of foreign trade under Qing control. The empire’s silver-based monetary economy depended on silver imports, largely from the Americas. In the early nineteenth century the flow reversed as rising opium imports drained silver abroad. The resulting deflationary pressures added to the fiscal strains of military expenditure and disaster relief, and weakened provincial administration just as foreign pressure intensified.
fields.military: The Qing military rested on the Eight Banners of Manchu, Mongol and Han bannermen that had conquered China, supplemented by the Green Standard Army, a much larger force of Han Chinese soldiers dispersed in smaller garrisons across the provinces. The Banner forces were maintained as a hereditary military caste on state stipends. They performed effectively while the empire was expanding but declined as hereditary entitlement replaced selection by merit, and their stipends absorbed growing revenues without a matching gain in military capacity. The Qianlong Emperor’s Ten Great Campaigns between the 1750s and 1792 were the height of Qing military power. They comprised the conquest of Dzungaria, the subjugation of the oasis cities of the Tarim Basin in Eastern Turkestan, campaigns in Burma, Vietnam and Nepal, the suppression of rebellion on Taiwan and the two Jinchuan wars in Sichuan, and they extended the empire to its greatest extent of some 13 to 14.7 million square kilometres by various estimates. The Dzungar campaigns of 1755–1758 almost completely destroyed the Dzungar Mongols through military violence, deliberate massacre and smallpox. Many historians characterise the episode as the Dzungar genocide, in which perhaps several hundred thousand people perished. The First Opium War of 1839–1842 exposed the inadequacy of Qing forces against industrialised European militaries: a British fleet with modern artillery and steam-powered warships such as the iron steamer Nemesis overcame Qing coastal and Yangtze defences and forced the Treaty of Nanjing.
fields.governance: The Qing administrative system adapted Ming bureaucratic institutions to the needs of Manchu minority rule over an overwhelmingly Han Chinese population. The dynasty retained the civil service examinations as the principal means of elite recruitment. Candidates were tested on the Confucian classics, and the highest jinshi degree qualified holders for senior office. The examinations preserved Chinese cultural tradition and won over the Confucian scholar-gentry, whose support was indispensable to stable government. A system of ethnic dyarchy placed Manchu and Han officials in paired senior posts in the central ministries, which ensured Manchu oversight while drawing on Han administrative expertise. The Grand Council, established by the Yongzheng Emperor around 1729 as a small inner body for urgent military and political matters, concentrated decision-making close to the emperor and bypassed the more cumbersome Grand Secretariat, so that government responded more quickly during the dynasty’s vigorous middle period. Inner Asian territories such as Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang were managed separately through the Lifan Yuan, the Court of Colonial Affairs, under arrangements that preserved local rulers and religious hierarchies. The Literary Inquisition reached its height under the Qianlong Emperor in connection with the great Siku Quanshu compilation. It condemned thousands of works as seditious and punished their authors or owners, and it reveals an anxiety beneath the dynasty’s confident exterior about the long-term security of Manchu rule over a far more numerous subject population.
fields.impact: The Qing Empire’s most lasting geopolitical effect was on China’s modern territorial extent. The incorporation of Xinjiang, Tibet, Mongolia, Taiwan and Manchuria into the Qing realm created the territorial framework on which the modern Chinese state, today the People's Republic of China, was largely built, although Outer Mongolia broke away after 1911. The empire was also an economic power. At its eighteenth-century peak, China is estimated to have produced around a third of the world’s manufactured goods, and European demand for Chinese silk, porcelain and tea drew silver from the Americas through Europe and the Pacific to China on a scale that affected global monetary flows. Chinese markets were forced open through the Opium Wars and the unequal treaty system, which granted foreign powers extraterritorial jurisdiction and treaty ports, fixed low import tariffs and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in 1842. This semi-colonial commercial penetration marked Chinese political consciousness deeply and fuelled the nationalism that drove Chinese politics in the twentieth century. The Taiping Rebellion of 1850–1864 was among the most destructive civil wars in human history, with an estimated twenty to thirty million deaths. It and the Muslim revolts that followed in the north-west showed how the Qing’s fiscal and military weakness created conditions for catastrophic internal violence, which changed the human geography of entire provinces.
fields.decline: The Qing Empire collapsed under the combined effects of fiscal weakness, military obsolescence, ecological and demographic stress, internal rebellion and sustained foreign imperial pressure from the mid-nineteenth century onwards. The White Lotus Rebellion of 1796–1804 and the later Taiping, Nian and Dungan rebellions between 1850 and 1877 consumed imperial revenues and destroyed agricultural infrastructure. They also showed that the Banner and Green Standard armies could not suppress large-scale insurgency without the Han Chinese regional armies, the Xiang Army of Zeng Guofan and the Huai Army of Li Hongzhang, whose success shifted real military power from the Manchu court to Han regional commanders. The Self-Strengthening Movement of the 1860s to 1890s attempted selective military and industrial modernisation, establishing arsenals, shipyards and schools, but its conservative framework left the political and educational system largely untouched. Defeat by Japan in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895 forced the cession of Taiwan and the recognition of Korean independence. It showed that a modernising Asian neighbour could overwhelm Qing forces, and it destroyed much of the dynasty’s remaining prestige among the educated elite. In 1898 the Empress Dowager Cixi suppressed the Hundred Days’ Reform, placing the reformist Guangxu Emperor under house arrest and executing six of his reformist allies; this ended the most ambitious internal attempt at systemic renewal. The disastrous Boxer Uprising of 1900 brought foreign occupation of Beijing and a crushing indemnity. The Xinhai Revolution of 1911 began with a military uprising at Wuchang and spread rapidly as provinces declared independence. It led to the abdication of the six-year-old Puyi on 12 February 1912, which ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China.
fields.summary: The Qing Empire was a dynasty that achieved the greatest territorial extent and one of the largest economies in Chinese history, yet it failed to develop the political institutions needed to meet the challenges of the modern world. It left its successors the boundaries of a very large nation and the unresolved tensions of a century of foreign encroachment, which marked China’s subsequent history.
fields.teaser: The Manchu Qing was China's last imperial dynasty (1644–1912). It expanded China to its greatest territorial extent before declining in the 19th century under Western pressure and large internal rebellions.
fields.t0: The Qing was a Manchu dynasty that conquered Ming China in 1644 and ruled the world's most populous empire.
fields.t1: It reached its greatest extent in the 18th century, setting the territorial framework of modern China.
fields.t2: Rebellion, defeat in the Opium Wars and by Japan, and failed reform led to revolution and Puyi's abdication in 1912.
fields.dyk: Nurhaci's Banner system organised the entire Jurchen population into colour-coded units that were at once army formations, census registers and social structures.
